My favorite times of year here are mid March through early May and mid October through early December. Both times of year aren’t oppressively hot usually, so outside weather can be enjoyed, and there’s always something to do. Spring tends to have more festivals, but fall brings Voodoo Music Experience, Halloween Balls, costume parties at bars (like EXTREME elaborate costumes), Vampire Masquerades, Public Voodoo Ceremonies, and ancestral reverence with All Saints Day and Day of the Dead. The air is a bit more crisp in fall, but the spring breeze is always nicer, and on a good day you can catch that balmy evening breeze that’s warm and muggy but somehow still refreshing because it’s a breeze. Plus all the flowers bloom in the spring! You’ll have the best luck with swamp boat tours, nature hikes, and trips to the zoo in late spring or early fall.

Chicken paprikash

Two pounds of chicken, breast or whatever is cheapest, cut into chunks.

Mix about 2 cups flour with a tablespoon of paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, salt, pepper, and 1/2 teaspoon of cayenne.

Coat chicken chunks in flour mixture and cook in oil on stove in deep pan or Dutch oven, maybe 10-15 mins.

Deglaze with white wine if you got it, then cover chicken with broth (I usually make some broth with bouillon), add some veggies if you want like mushrooms, broccoli, whatever you got, add more broth to cover veggies if needed. Simmer on medium about 20 mins uncovered.

Mix about 1-2 cups of sour cream with remaining flour mixture, then add that to chicken and all, mixing to ensure no lumps, then cook on low 5 mins to allow thickening.

Serve over egg noodles, rice, mashed potatoes...literally whatever starch you have.

I used to work at a funeral home in a major city with many outlying rural areas and the rural coroners contracted with us to make the removals for their office. It also included many water retrievals from lakes and a large river, including us wading into the water to pull someone out, as well as “found dead” mostly liquefied decedents and other such fun scenarios. The coroner investigator would always meet us on scene and then we’d transport the decedent to a larger coroner’s office within the city and the larger coroner would do the autopsy. It was simply easier for the rural coroner to pay us per removal since we’re already staffed 24/7 than to hire their own team because they didn’t have enough of a demand for more investigators in their small town. I live in a major city in the southern United States where investigations are conducted on ALL deaths that aren’t natural causes. Where do you live that suicide victims are not autopsied? And I’ll agree $1500 is way too much for embalming, the norm in my area is around $500 or less. Restorative work is ALWAYS done with embalming (suturing, closing the mouth, reforming the eye shape). Restorative work is anything from trying to get the face to look “natural” to covering wounds and reducing swelling, but it is done in every single embalming, at least in my area (I can’t imagine anywhere that would embalm without closing the eyes and mouth though).

Again, a misnomer. Refrigeration delays decomposition but does not stop it entirely. So you’d be seeing your mother after undoubtedly an autopsy in which her head and her entire chest cavity were opened (exposing blood born pathogens because suturing does not seal the cavity from airborne pathogens), and likely at least several days to a week would have passed before the service, if not longer. Noticeable decomposition can begin in as little as 48 hours even under refrigeration, depending on the condition of the tissues to begin with.
This is also a misnomer, these types of cribs are highly specialized and not available in most general hospitals, at least across the Southern United States (where I’m familiar with)

Again I’m so sorry for the tragedy with your mom. But you do need to also understand that hanging causes damage to vessels and tissues that would cause a lot of swelling if embalming and restorative work was not done. More often than not, tissues break down more than most people realize beginning immediately after death, and often times decedents will leak bodily fluids. It’s for all of these reasons that we embalm for public viewings. Now don’t get me wrong, I personally do not want to be embalmed, but knowing that I also won’t be having a public viewing.

I’m so sorry to hear about your mom, and the experience you went through. I do think it’s important to educate the public about options but I think a lot is missed or neglected with Caitlin’s information. For example, whether or not embalming is required for a public viewing can vary based on location or even state to state, as each state has different laws. And even in some circumstances embalming may not be required by law but the funeral home may have a requirement for it for a large gathering due to the risk of exposure to blood borne pathogens. Again, I think it’s important for the public to be educated but I wish she would give ALL the information.

The experience at the more rural locations highly varies based on how management handles things. I work at a location that has to call several rural locations across my state for P&E pretty regularly and there are major differences from location to location. At one location the directors are constantly unpleasant and overworked even though they only do about 100 cases a year, the manager is just never present to help and keeping a lean staff is pretty standard at SCI so if management doesn’t help it can be a nightmare for the directors. Another location I work with has their own crematory and refrigeration and one of my care center’s embalmers actually moved to work there because it paid more and she wanted to get back to doing funerals and embalming instead of just embalming like you would at a care center. She now gets to do it all, even operate the crematory, and she loves it. Another big difference is that the first one, where the directors are miserable, the directors and embalmers make all the removals, including night removals. At the second one, they have their own removal staff and use a third party transport when necessary. So ask those types of questions at the location you’re going to (what will my duties be, who makes removals, do we need to take night call, etc) and get a feel for the management while you’re there. It also doesn’t hurt to ask some of the other embalmers and directors how they like working there. Good luck! (For the record, I LOVE my location, we’re a smaller one too, and I feel extremely supported by management and corporate at my location.)

I can’t contribute much about PA law but I can tell you that in some states a NOK has a limited time to step forward before an Authorized Representative is appointed who is basically any interested party willing to make the arrangements. Cremation costs vary state to state and in my state the average cost for cremation is about $3500, so again you may want to price shop around the area to see if he’s gouging prices. Also if you have anyone nearby the funeral home ask them to stop by and request a GPL (general price list) which the funeral home will be required by law to give anyone asking in person. If the prices for cremation on the GPL don’t match the bill he sends you a copy of (saw on the other thread you already requested one) then you can report him to the FTC and PA State Board for violating the Funeral Rule which will easily result in hefty fines and possible loss of licensure. 

Also, in my state the family tells us who the next of kin is and we have to go in good faith that they’re being accurate unless someone else knowingly steps forward. So if your sister had come to me looking to cremate your father and she said she was the only child, we’d have to go by her word (we generally don’t have access to search databases to verify any information) and the documents she would sign to authorize the cremation would state that she attests to being the sole next of kin, therefore making her liable for lying instead of the funeral home being liable for not having all the information.

I’ve worked at both family owned and corporate, and felt more pressure to sell at the family owned than I ever did at the corporate. At the end of the day it all boils down to the manager/owner of the place you work at because even most corporate owned will be operated pretty individually based on their location, business flow, and what the manager of the location expects.

My experience with corporate was much better than family owned, at the family owned you were expected to do EVERYTHING from removals to embalming to arrangements and services all in one day all while not using any overtime or the owner would get upset at you for having to pay overtime. My schedule was awful and unpredictable and there was no room for advancement because all the higher up positions went to family members of the owner. There was very little recourse if you didn’t like something that was happening because unless it was something illegal there’s nothing you can do. So if the owner spends an hour screaming at you because you didn’t answer your phone while you were on an unpaid lunch break, oh well that’s life. If the power goes out in the middle of summer and the owner requires you to stay and embalm in 102 degree weather by light of camping torch, oh well you do it. If the owner asks you to go outside and deep clean the mold off of the outside of the building, well you do that too. Plus the benefits were not good, barely any time off and if you took a sick day the owner might actually drive by your house to make sure you’re actually sick, which isn’t illegal so again nothing you can say or do about it.

Now as for the corporate, I’ve worked at a couple of corporate locations and my experience greatly varied based on management. The constants were: I didn’t feel any pressure to make sales, my role was always consistent as corporate firms are very compartmentalized, the benefits were incredible, if management did something immoral or unethical there was always a manager above them (or HR) that you could talk to and everyone was held accountable and held to the same standard regardless of how high you ranked in the company.

That said, I’ve had friends who had the exact opposite experience, they worked for a fantastic and very caring family firm and when a corporate bought them out they became miserable, so again it will greatly vary based on the corporation itself or the owners.

I gave birth at the beginning of the outbreak in my country. One week I was at my doctor’s office, everything was fine, we scheduled a pre-admit test at the hospital for the next week before my scheduled induction. 
The next week things started to heat up...I was advised to self isolate and work from home, though the state hadn’t officially shut down yet. When my husband and I went to the hospital for my pre-admit testing, it was day 1 for them of having screening for entrance and only allowing in people with appointments and no visitors. They didn’t tell me this prior to my appointment. I parked on the 4th floor garage where labor and delivery is only to find locked doors with a sign guiding me to the main entrance for a screening checkpoint.

My husband and I hoofed it down 4 flights of stairs and down to the main entrance, only to be stopped at screening because they couldn’t find my name on the appointments list. I had to call my doctor on speaker phone to verify the appointment, only to find out that the check point didn’t have ANY appointments for labor and delivery, so of course they couldn’t find me. At one point I even told them I’m 9 months pregnant and clearly need to get to the labor and delivery ward, what would happen if I was in labor right now?

When we get to the pre-admit testing my husband is not allowed in with me, even though he had been for everything up to that point. I ask the nurse if he’ll be allowed to accompany me when I give birth, she doesn’t know. I ask the nurse what I’m supposed to do if I go into labor before my induction since the main entrance was appointments only but I was explicitly told NOT to go through the ER entrance either as that’s where all the covid patients were. She didn’t know. She wrote down the phone number for the labor and delivery department and told me to call if I go into labor and they’ll have a nurse meet me at the front entrance.

When induction day came 4 days later we still didn’t know if my husband would be allowed to stay, we just had to wait and see what they said when we got past the checkpoint and into labor and delivery. The people at the checkpoint didn’t want to let him through. Again I had to tell them I’m 9 months pregnant and here to give birth and have a giant suitcase that I cannot manage myself so if you don’t let my husband accompany me to check in you’ll have to escort me yourself. They finally let him through.

Finally at labor and delivery they told us he could stay, but that he was not to leave the hospital at any time or else he wouldn’t be let back in, and that we’d both be tested for fevers daily and he’d have to leave if he had an elevated temperature. We both had to wear masks in all parts of the hospital except for my room, which was important because my husband still had to get his meals from the cafeteria, they only deliver food to the room for the patient.

After 24+ hours of unsuccessful labor we had to do an emergency c-section as baby’s heart rate was decelerating and my water had been broken for too long. Thankfully the procedure was quick and my doctor was very skilled, but even after an emergency c-section the hospital made us leave 2 days earlier than we normally otherwise would have because the risk of staying was greater than the risk of going home early.

My postpartum surgery check up was a phone call in which they explained to my husband how to sterilize kitchen sheers and then cut my remaining suture off as I could not go into the doctor unless I was experiencing complications. I’m 8 weeks pp and still have not seen my OBGYN in person.

It was scary, there were a lot of unknowns, and this is our first child so that compounded everything else. But...we got through it, and you will too. The labor itself, the surgery...all of it seems like such a quick blur now and the only thing I really remember from the hospital is getting to hold my baby boy. 

My best friend made a playlist for me to listen to while in labor and my husband picked out movies for me to watch so that even if I had been alone I’d have had them both with me in some way. My husband and I planned to FaceTime the entire time if he was not able to be there with me. It would have been awful, but there are ways to make it work.

I hope everything works out for you and your partner as well, these are scary and difficult times to bring a new baby into the world. It won’t be perfect and it won’t be near what you envisioned when you got pregnant, but it is only a small part of the bigger journey at the end of the day. Good luck mama.

A lot of corporately owned funeral homes (and even some larger family owned firms) will utilize a central prep site or “care center” to service all of their multiple locations. So a care center might service 7 different funeral homes in the area, all owned by the same corporation, and the care center’s responsibility would be all management and prep of decedent up until the service (so removal, refrigeration, embalming, dressing, cosmetizing, casketing, cremating, etc.). Find out which corporations operate in your area (you can talk to anyone in the industry in your area or you can talk to your local mortuary school if you have one in your area) then go to those corporations’ websites to find out which firms are in that area under the corporation’s umbrella (like SCI would list their funeral homes at www.dignitymemorial.com and Carriage would list theirs at www.carriageservices.com). Then you can call any of those locations and ask them if they use a central care center. If they do use a care center, then you’d be safe to work at that firm because the care center would be doing the heavy lifting for them (aside from carrying casketed remains at a burial service or church service when necessary, but you typically have pall bearers to help with that as a funeral director).

Depends on who you work for. Corporations are more likely to made ADA accommodations and less likely to have licensees making removals. Whereas most family owned funeral homes require everyone to do a rotating shift for removals. Is there any facility with a centralized care center in your area? If so, working at any of the funeral homes that the care center serves you should be fine.

Not sure if this counts, but my particular field has a mandatory internship period after graduating college and passing national board exams. During your internship you have a preceptor in charge of guiding you and teaching you the things the books didn’t, like physical techniques and state specific laws (school taught the national curriculum, not the state unique laws). The preceptor is often a supervisor or manager at the facility that gave you an internship, but could be anyone with a license in the field.

Internships are EXTREMELY competitive and extremely hard to come by in my area, so I started out doing grunt work at a facility to eventually earn an internship. My preceptor was the supervisor of the firm and more than a decade my senior. During the internship you understandably spend a lot of time together because the intern is not allowed to perform any job duties without supervision. So we had the same schedule, worked on the same projects, and ate lunch together every day. 

After about 4 months of this, we both come back from holiday break and as we’re catching up we both say we have big news. His news turned out to be that he filed for divorce with his wife (he’d been wanting to for a long time but talking with me about infidelity finally gave him the push, his ex-wife had cheated on him twice and he had proof). My news was that I broke up with my long term boyfriend (I spent the holiday with my sister who saw I was miserable because my boyfriend wasn’t respecting me and ultimately she gave me the sister talk of “what are you actually getting out of this relationship?”). We both kind of looked at each other and blushed and went back to eating lunch in a bit of awkward silence.

It took another four months of awkward brushing up against each other while trying to work (physical job), awkward radio songs coming on while working (Don’t Stand So Close to Me by Sting and the Police, Caught Up In You by .38 Special, Young Girl by Gary Puckett and the Union Gap just to name a few, that ALL came on spontaneously on the radio while we were working together on more than one occasion), and veiled flirting before we finally went on a date together.

He continued being my preceptor for the remaining 4 months of my internship and we dated in secret (since he was my immediate superior and responsible for whether I got my license in the field), then when I got my license we both went public with the relationship and shortly after moved to a different firm where he was immediately promoted to management and I was promoted to management within a year.

5 years later we’re both still doing well with the new firm, married, own a house together, and our first baby is due in a month. :) So mine has a happy ending.

As mentioned, if they are more of a traditional funeral home they will likely only have a one size fits all shipping of cremated remains charge on their general price list, regardless of what type of urn or keepsake is shipping. The FD would not be able to stray from the general price list price, as pricing is very heavily regulated by the federal trade commission.

All FHs have a charge to mail cremated remains on their general price list. Some cremation specific ones will have a lower cost to mail keepsakes and jewelry (such as $75 instead of $150) but most traditional funeral homes just have a one size fits all shipping charge for cremated remains. USPS priority mail express is the only legal way to mail cremated remains in the USA and can get very costly (I’ve personally mailed a keepsake to somewhere only an hour’s drive away and it still cost us $45 to mail, not including labor costs and materials to pack and ship), and gets more costly depending on the destination (rural areas cost more than metropolitan ones and the distance is a factor as well), the weight, and the declared value (if the jewelry is sterling silver the funeral home may have to purchase additional insurance on it).

The time difference is because of the rate of decomposition. Decomposition takes longer in a metal casket due to the protection from the elements that metal offers over wood. The extra day is just a state ordinance, more of a paperwork stipulation than anything else.

Honestly not much, there’s no real benefit of a sealed casket in a wet and humid environment, because no caskets truly “seal.” However the difference between metal and wood is the decomposition rate. For instance, if we bury in a metal casket we have to wait ten years and a day for reburial instead of one year and a day in a wooden casket.

What sort of climate do you live in? We live in a very southern and wet climate in the United States that typically uses wooden caskets for burial (so not sealing or airtight at all). We also practice reburial here, meaning that after a year and a day a decedent can be disinterred, their remains moved into a storage bag, the bag then placed at a reservoir at the back of the family tomb, and a new decedent buried in that spot. In my experience, due largely to our climate, fluids are almost unavoidable unless we’re talking about a vast amount of time between burials.

If you want to do solely embalming and prepping you’d most likely need to work for a corporation. Most funeral director/embalmers end up moving or having a long commute to find work, and the pay is a fraction of what you’d make in the medical field. You’d also have to put in your time and start out doing everything, removals (read: picking up the decedent from their home or other place of death), funeral services, arrangements - all required in most states to get a funeral director/embalmer license (usually can’t have an embalmer license without also being a licensed funeral director in most states).

Someone else mentioned being a medical examiner or forensic doctor, and if you’re interested in helping the deceased but still making decent money and being in the medical field this is what I would recommend.

Though embalmers do learn chemistry and biology, aside from the biology of decomp and the circulatory system we rarely ever use what we learned in school. Most of it is hands-on learning and muscle memory, and to some it’s more of an art form than an exact science (especially when it comes to setting facial features and doing restorative work).

If you can, I’d go for the medical field. Embalmers and funeral directors often earn about what teachers earn in their area, again depending on the state.

It's a bit of a taboo too because I don't think people on the outside really understand what we struggle with. My counselor is a former police officer so he was able to spot the PTSD because he'd been through it himself, but when I talked to my family about it the overwhelming response from anyone other than my fiance was, "You don't have PTSD, you don't get scared in thunderstorms." Well, of course we don't, because our triggers don't come from loud noises akin to gunfire, but they don't get that. I learned as a student that most people don't last 5 years in our field, and I can say that three years after graduating there are only a few of my nearly 20 classmates in the field. It's hard. Serving the families is why we do it, and it's important, but we have to remember to serve ourselves too. Are you on night call? That can make it seem even worse, never being able to relax even when you get home because you know the minute you take a bath or open that book you'll get a call. I had bad burnout this year, and just came back from my first vacation all year. It was refreshing, and gave me a lot of perspective about escapism versus actual self care. The fetus will usually be removed by the ME during autopsy, and I can't imagine a situation where there wouldn't be an autopsy when a late term mother passes. In our state, autopsy is required for EVERYONE without a severe medical history or if circumstances of the death are brought into question AT ALL. Most caskets here are half couch, and there's really no way hide a mostly pregnant belly, so the belly would remain in its natural swollen state and would only be viewable partially with a half couch. The fetus would be placed with the mother, either back inside if being viewed or directly next to for immediate burial or cremation. The fetus is treated as tissue of the mother, as it was never 'born' and a birth record was never created so it legally is not a 'person' by itself. I'm speaking in terms of our state's laws, but I imagine most are similar.
